newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa threatened by strike in pay row.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa threatened by strike in pay row.

text.p: German airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG on Monday faced a possible all-out strike by some of its staff next month after one of its main unions said it would be proceeding with plans to call a strike ballot.

The DAG white-collar union, which shares representation of the airline's some 50,000 staff with the OeTV public sector and transport union, said it would be balloting ground- and aircrew on their readiness to strike over the next three to four weeks.

DAG said in a statement that it had hoped the two limited walk-outs carried out by staff late last year would be enough to persuade the airline to reconsider its pay offer, which is based around a 1.7 percent 1997 wage increase.

A Lufthansa spokesman said however that the airline, which is seeking to reduce its costs in the face of increased competition by foreign airlines along its domestic routes, would not be pressurised into changing its position. "We are working on the assumption that the result of the ballot will take between four to six weeks. We shall use that time to continue to explain to our employees our point of view concerning the strategic and commercial future of the airline," a Lufthansa spokesman said by telephone.
Earlier two-hour walk-outs by Lufthansa staff -- the maximum duration allowed under German labour law -- have already cost the airline some 30 million marks in lost business.
If a full strike is to go ahead, the union needs to get the support of 70 percent of its members at the airline.

DAG, which is seeking a pay rise for 1997 around four percent, said it hoped its action would convince Lufthansa to make a one-year pay agreement offering a pay rise in line with others in the sector.

DAG deputy chairman Hubert Gartz said that his union was not prepared to accept a pay agreement running over 27 months as sought by the airline, adding that this was not in line with the performance of the airline's workers.

"The DAG has already proved in the past that it is responsible in its wage policies at Lufthansa and does not lose sight of the competitiveness of the company," he said, referring in particular to pay sacrifices made in 1992.
Outside its 1.7 percent annual wage rise, Lufthansa has offered a one-off payment of 33 percent of a monthly salary plus a payment of 500 marks cash or 625 marks in Lufthansa shares.
